item.title: Frontier breaks ground on Waroona solar and battery project
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Frontier Energy has broken ground on the first stage of its Waroona Renewable Energy Project in Western Australia – a 132 MW solar facility paired with an 81.5 MW / 6.9-hour battery energy storage system.
item.content:encoded:
Perth-based clean energy developer Frontier Energy announced major construction has commenced on Stage One of its flagship Waroona Renewable Energy Project in southwest Western Australia with first generation scheduled for 2028.

The first stage of the project, located about 120 kilometres south of state capital Perth, comprises a 132 MW solar facility and an 81.5 MW / 6.9-hour battery energy storage system. The DC-coupled system has been designed to capture solar energy during the day and dispatch electricity into the grid during periods of high-value demand.

Frontier Chief Executive Officer Adam Kiley said the project – that will connect to WA’s main electricity network, the South West Interconnected System (SWIS), via the nearby 330 kV Landwehr Terminal – will make a major contribution to the state’s clean energy transition, with the first stage of the project forecast to replace a third of the power generated by the coal-fired Collie power station that is due to close in 2027.

“When energy generation commences in 2028, our Waroona project will become the largest solar and battery hybrid facility connected to WA’s main electricity network and will be a major part in helping the state reach its target of 75% renewable energy by 2031,” he said, adding that the company’s intent is to develop Waroona into a multi-stage renewable energy hub.

“Stage One is only the beginning for Frontier, as we aim to expand beyond Stage One and establish the Waroona project as a major renewable energy hub in the heart of southwest WA, bringing much-needed new generation onto the grid in an area that has been supported by coal for more than 60 years,” he said.

Beyond Stage One, Frontier intends to expand the development significantly. Its longer-term ambition targets approximately 1 GW of solar generation and 660 MW of battery storage by 2031.

Stage Two already has development approval and proposes approximately 120 MW of solar generation alongside 80 MW of battery storage.

Western Australian contractor Monford Group holds the fixed-price engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contract for the first stage of the Waroona project. Its responsibilities include constructing and commissioning the integrated solar and battery facility.

Chinese manufacturer Longi has been tapped to supply the solar modules, while Trina Storage will provide the battery system. Nextpower will supply solar tracking equipment, with SMA Australia providing inverters.

Major construction works include field piling for installation of the single access tracking system, followed by installation of the PV modules and construction of the solar facility balance of plant, which is scheduled to commence in early 2027.

The start of construction proper on the Waroona project comes after Frontier earlier this month executed a syndicated facility agreement for project finance debt facilities of up to $280 million (USD 194 million) provided by a syndicate of international lenders led by France-headquartered investment bank Natixis CIB and Japanese financial services conglomerate Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation.

The company has also executed its Capacity Investment Scheme agreement with the Australian government which provides a minimum level of guaranteed revenue support for the project until 2042.

Frontier has also been assigned capacity credits for stage one of the Waroona project as part of the Australian Energy Market Operator’s Reserve Capacity Mechanism. The fixed five-year agreement ensures revenue certainty of circa $160 million for the project.

item.title: New glass-to-glass PV module design enables rapid delamination
item.dc:creator: Lior Kahana
item.description: An international research team has developed an induction heating-assisted method to separate end-of-life solar modules in seconds. The process enables the recovery of up to 99.8% of module mass, including glass, silicon cells and encapsulants.
item.content:encoded:
An international research team, including scientists from the University of New South Wales (UNSW), has developed an induction heating-assisted delamination method for end-of-life PV modules to improve recyclability and facilitate the recovery of individual components.

“We designed a glass-glass photovoltaic module that is easier to take apart at the end of its life,” corresponding author Yonghwan Lee told pv magazine. “Using induction heating, we rapidly separated the layers of our test module and recovered 99.8% of its original mass, including the glass, the silicon cell and the polymer encapsulant.”

Lee said the team was surprised by how quickly and cleanly the silicon cell separated using the new technique and modified module design.

“In our fastest test, the module layers separated in just five seconds. We recovered the cell intact, with no visible polymer residue on its surface, without having to remove the entire encapsulant layer first,” he said.

The researchers first used Comsol Multiphysics simulations to investigate induction heating in passivated emitter and rear contact (PERC) cells and heat transfer through the surrounding module layers. They examined the effects of operating frequency, coil current, coil-to-cell distance and electrode thickness on heating.

They then produced simplified samples comprising a 2 cm × 2 cm PERC cell laminated onto tempered glass with ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulant, leaving the rear of the cell exposed. They tested the method using a water-cooled copper induction coil operating at 270 kHz to 300 kHz to rapidly heat the cell’s metal contacts, triggering localised EVA decomposition at the cell-encapsulant interface. The samples were suspended with the cells facing downward to enable gravity-assisted separation.

The tests showed that induction heating created a temperature difference of more than 200 C between the cell and glass at a coil current of 100 A, enabling localised EVA decomposition at the cell interface. With gravity-assisted separation, the cells detached in approximately 14 seconds.

Microscopy revealed no significant polymer residue or structural damage on the recovered cell surfaces, while spectroscopy indicated that the remaining EVA largely retained its chemical structure.

The researchers then fabricated modified glass-glass mini-modules incorporating a single PERC cell, EVA encapsulant and two tempered glass sheets measuring 5 cm × 8 cm and 1 mm thick. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) release films, each with a central opening measuring 1.8 cm × 1.8 cm, were inserted between the cell and EVA on both sides to allow gases generated during heating to escape. The researchers suspended the mini-modules in a custom support jig and applied induction heating at coil currents of 100 A, 150 A and 200 A.

The modified mini-modules separated in 18.6 seconds at a coil current of 100 A, compared with 8.3 seconds at 150 A and 5.4 seconds at 200 A. The process recovered 99.8% of the total module mass, with negligible losses of glass, cells and release films.

After delamination, the researchers mechanically scraped the EVA from the glass, resulting in less than 10% encapsulant mass loss. Analysis of the recovered cells showed no significant surface residue.

“For us, this points to a way to recycle modules quickly and brings the goal of 100% material recovery closer,” Lee said. “Our next step is to apply the process to full-size commercial PV panels and scale it up for use in commercial recycling operations.”

The researchers presented their findings in “Inductive heating for photovoltaic module recycling and near-complete component recovery,” which was published in Communications Materials. The research team included scientists from South Korea’s Korea Electronics Technology Institute (KETI) and Australia’s UNSW.

item.title: DMEGC launches steel-framed solar module series
item.dc:creator: Emiliano Bellini
item.description: The new series of n-type bifacial solar modules features a steel frame with an S-shaped cross-section. The modules deliver 640 W to 665 W of power output and offer a bifaciality factor of up to 85%, with the new frame design reportedly reducing rear-side shading by 76%.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese solar manufacturer DMEGC has unveiled a new series of bifacial glass-glass PV modules featuring a steel frame designed to improve mechanical reliability and rear-side power generation.

“The zinc-aluminum-magnesium (Zn-Al-Mg) coated steel used in the frames has nearly twice the tensile strength of conventional aluminum alloys, enabling the modules to withstand snow loads of up to 6,000 Pa and wind loads of up to 5,000 Pa when installed with suitable mounting systems,” a spokesperson from the company told pv magazine.

DMEGC said the material also has a lower coefficient of thermal expansion, compared with aluminum and glass. The closer thermal expansion characteristics of steel and glass could reduce mechanical stress and the risk of cell microcracks during temperature fluctuations, the company said.

The frame features an S-shaped cross-section that reportedly reduces vertical shading on the rear side of the module by 76% compared with conventional frame designs. DMEGC said the geometry increases the unshaded rear-side area by 3.6%, resulting in a theoretical improvement in bifaciality of approximately 2.8%.

The new Infinity RT 3.0 series comprises six models with power outputs ranging from 640 W to 665 W and efficiencies between 23.7% and 24.6%.

The DMxxxG12RT-B66HSW 640~665W modules are based on 132 n-type monocrystalline half-cut cells and measure 2,382 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm, with a weight of 33.3 kg. They feature 2 mm heat-strengthened glass on both sides and are designed for utility-scale PV applications.

The modules achieve a bifaciality factor of up to 85%, according to the manufacturer. DMEGC’s energy yield simulations indicate annual electricity generation of 2,078 kWh/kWp, corresponding to a 0.6% increase in generation revenue compared with conventional modules under the simulated conditions.

The modules feature a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V and an operating temperature range of -40 C to 85 C. Their temperature coefficient is -0.28%/C, while the nominal module operating temperature is 42 C.

DMEGC said the products have undergone salt mist and ammonia corrosion testing, as well as extended stress testing.

The manufacturer offers a 15-year product warranty and a 30-year linear power output warranty. It guarantees no more than 1% degradation in the first year and a maximum annual degradation rate of 0.35% thereafter, with a guaranteed power output of 88.85% after 30 years.

From pv magazine Global

item.title: Rural Australian communities are hosting the clean energy boom. Are they getting a fair say?
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Australia’s transition to clean energy is happening at pace, with regional areas front and centre. Rural communities are being asked to host the wind farms, solar panels and transmission lines to power our biggest cities – sometimes hundreds of kilometres away.
item.content:encoded:
Accommodating these large developments can be burdensome for small communities. Projects can impact farmland and load local roads. They can also pile more pressure on housing and essential services.

To sweeten the deal, affected communities are being promised a once-in-a-generation wave of investment, touted as an economic lifeline for many regional towns struggling to survive.

Not everyone is buying the promise. With a state election looming, Victoria offers some stark examples of how these tensions are playing out.

Some councils have been sidelined by the state government in key decisions. Planning laws have been changed to fast-track projects. In many areas, community backlash has been fierce.

These tensions point to questions that go beyond any individual project. Are regional communities being given a meaningful say in their economic future? And will they actually be left better off?

Big changes are coming

For regional Australia, the scale of change is enormous. So, too, is the economic opportunity it presents.

The Australian Energy Market Operator has estimated that achieving net zero emissions will require $106 billion (USD 72 billion) in new investment (in today’s dollars) by 2050. This includes investment in 6,000 kilometres of new transmission lines across the country.

This money is already flowing. According to the Clean Energy Council, 141 clean energy projects worth about $32.5 billion were financed or already under construction in the first half of this year.

A noisy, confusing picture

One of the biggest challenges for communities is navigating this rapidly evolving landscape. Each state and territory is taking a different approach to these developments – not only for renewable energy but also for critical minerals and mining more broadly.

Take Victoria, for example. VicGrid and the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action recently released community engagement and social value guidelines. These set minimum expectations for engagement with and benefits for communities and landowners who host projects, but (unlike in New South Wales) no minimum dollar-per-megawatt figure.

The guidelines only cover renewable energy and transmission projects, but exclude projects connecting to the local distribution network. Separate compensation arrangements apply to some transmission projects, adding to the complexity.

Initially voluntary, these guidelines only become mandatory in mid-2027, when the extent of collaboration between developers will also be assessed.

Importantly, and perhaps confusingly, they do not cover critical mineral projects. These are covered by separate legislation and still-to-be-determined community benefit payments.

In short, it is a noisy, confusing and dynamic landscape for communities and landowners.

Yet some regional communities are taking matters into their own hands and electing to shape their own energy destiny. In north-west Victoria, for example, Wimmera Southern Mallee Development has been working with energy developers and various government agencies through its Renewable Energy Collaboration partnership.

Not everyone is on board

Victoria again offers some striking examples of vocal community opposition.

There’s been sustained backlash from farmers against the Victoria to NSW Interconnector West (VNI West) transmission project in north-west Victoria, which the state opposition have vowed to scrap if elected.

And in the north of the state, intense community backlash recently convinced the government to abandon a plan to create a new renewable energy zone around Dookie.

This month, Australian Public Policy Institute research (of which I was a coauthor) casts light on some of these concerns for rural Australia more broadly.

This drew on workshops and interviews conducted with a broad range of stakeholders in three towns in regional NSW impacted by renewable energy development. We found affected communities broadly support the shift to clean energy.

However, key community concerns are already delaying the process. This threatens to to undermine the long-term energy transition.

Why communities are wary

Assessing these responses, we found three big challenges for the government and industry.

First, community consultation and engagement were seen as inconsistent and often inadequate. Further, there were limited opportunities for communities, including First Nations people, to meaningfully influence project planning and decision-making.

Second, communication and planning processes lacked transparency, clarity and a place-based focus.

And third, communities are experiencing significant social and economic impacts. Benefit-sharing and compensation arrangements were viewed as inequitable, insufficiently targeted and lacking long-term community value.

Bridging all of these challenges, we found trust in industry, government and the planning system was fragile.

What communities want

Encouragingly, however, we also found regional participants in NSW were keen to provide detailed policy solutions for governments to address many of these challenges.

They called for four key changes.

First, minimum, enforceable engagement standards should be required for all major energy projects. These standards should prioritise transparency, accountability and building trust.

Second, governments should work with communities to develop a framework on sharing of benefits. This should then be embedded into planning regulations.

Third, there should be more support and resources for communities to help with negotiating how project benefits are shared.

And fourth, at all levels of government, planning processes and governance should adopt a place-based approach tailored to local needs.

Building trust

Increasingly for Australia, the main barriers to a successful shift to renewable energy are not technical but social.

Many rural and regional communities feel excluded from decisions about how the transition will be achieved. Importantly, communities are not rejecting the transition. They are asking for better information and communication, fairer benefits, and a genuine role in shaping the changes that affect them.

*

Author: Simon Wright, Senior Research Fellow, Energy & Circularity, Gulbali Institute, Charles Sturt University.

This article was initially published in The Conversation and is republished here under a Creative Commons Licence.

item.title: 260 MW solar project part of AirTrunk, European Energy deal
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: A 260 MW solar project and 800 MWh battery energy storage system in the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone
item.content:encoded:
Danish clean energy developer European Energy Australia has signed an exclusivity agreement with Blackstone-led consortium-owned Sydney-headquartered hyperscale data centre company AirTrunk to progress renewable energy projects in the Hunter region of New South Wales (NSW).

The proposed projects include a 260 MW solar project and 800 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS), and a 350 MWp wind project in the Hunter-Central Renewable Energy Zone (REZ) located north of Sydney between 150-250 kilometres across the REZ.

Anticipating commercial operation of the solar and battery projects by 2030, the companies are in discussions about a potential long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) to support AirTrunk’s NSW energy requirements, including for its proposed $3.7 billion (USD 2.5 billion), 44,220 square metre, two-storey 550 MW Kurri Kurri data centre campus in the Hunter Valley on the former Kurri Kurri smelter site at Loxford.

AirTrunk AVP Energy Sabooh Whitelaw said the company is focussed on bringing new renewable generation forward and securing renewable electricity through long-term supply arrangements.

 “The Hunter projects are an important step, but more renewable generation and firming will be needed to support Kurri Kurri and AirTrunk’s wider NSW needs,” Whitelaw said.

“We’ll continue working with developers and energy partners to progress further projects across Australia”.

European Energy Australia Managing Director Catriona McLeod noted the importance of AirTrunk and the tech sector more broadly, embracing renewable energy.

“Partnerships like this allow us to bring more renewables online and add more energy to the grid.”

“The partnership builds on AirTrunk and European Energy Australia’s work at the 31 MW Mulwala Solar Farm, which officially opened this week and is now supplying renewable electricity to NSW’s grid. The companies will continue to explore further renewable energy opportunities.”

AirTrunk Founder and CEO Robin Khuda said digital growth must bring new energy with it.

“The Australian government’s expectations and NSW’s guidelines set a high bar for the industry. This partnership is an important step towards delivering on that commitment,” Khuda said.

item.title: Wollemi Capital buys stake in US solar developer Redball Energy
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Australian growth investor Wollemi Capital and superannuation fund Rest have acquired a majority stake in US-headquartered distributed solar developer Redball Energy.
item.content:encoded:
In its first foray in the US energy market, Sydney-headquartered growth investor Wollemi Capital and Retail Employees Superannation Trust (Rest) fund have acquired a majority stake in US-headquartered owner and operator of distributed solar assets Redball Energy.

Washington-based Redball owns and operates approximately 4,500 rooftop solar systems on homes and businesses in the Mid-Atlantic and New England regions, which include Maine, New Hampshire and New York.

It does not sell or install panels directly to homeowners but provides project financing, streamlined payments and asset owership.

The investment supports Redball’s next phase of growth to expand its installer partner network, continue its selective expansion in its current markets and broaden its offering to include battery storage.

Wollemi Capital US Co-Head Natalie Volpe said Wollemi Capital US Co-Head Natalie Volpe said Redball was a natural fit with Wollemi’s strategic focus on backing real asset portfolios that are proven, distributed and scalable.

“The Redball team has built an impressive business through a disciplined, partnership-led approach, and the opportunity for distributed energy in the US is significant as electricity demand rises,” Volpe said.

“We’re excited to partner with Redball and bring our experience backing distributed solar and storage platforms to the US market.”

Redball Co-Founder John Marciano said the company seeks overlooked opportunities in the energy transition and back the teams bringing clean energy projects to market at scale.

“In Wollemi [we’ve] found a partner who shares that vision and will help take Redball to the next level, as America’s need for affordable energy and resilient, distributed infrastructure continues to grow.”

On 2 November 2026, Rest announced it had expanded its total commitment to $250 million (USD 170 million) for Wollemi Energy Group-owned Sydney-based energy and battery storage platform MPower.

It follows a $220 million commitment to Wollemi in 2025. At that time Rest Private Markets General Manager Marina Pasika said the commitment to Wollemi, and MPower, would generate long-term returns for members given Wollemi’s approach to advancing decarbonisation.

“Many of our members have decades until retirement, including around one million under 30, so we look for investment opportunities that can support members throughout their lives, while benefitting from the major economic and societal shifts expected to shape the future,” Pasika said.

item.title: Three minute battery cell health check could transform recycling and second-life potential
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Researchers at UNSW, Sydney have developed a battery health test that is 95.5% faster than existing testing, over 80% cheaper, and has the potential to both increase second-life battery use and keep significant battery waste from landfill.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers from the University of New South Wales (UNSW), Sydney have developed a prototype to test battery health, that is 95.5% faster than existing testing and over 80% cheaper, with implications for reducing landfill and improving second-life use.

Designed to work with the management systems already used by recyclers and energy storage operators, the platform will assess the three main lithium-ion chemistries used in electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage: lithium iron phosphate (LFP), nickel cobalt aluminium (NCA) and nickel manganese cobalt (NMC).

Current used-battery testing relies on an approximately 10-hour full charge-discharge process, which can lead to overheating and fire if damaged batteries endure hours of high-stress cycling. It also costs around $120 (USD 85) per EV battery pack.

Instead, the UNSW prototype platform uses short electrical pulses through each battery cell, and measures how cells respond. Statistical models then estimate the battery’s health in under three minutes per cell, with lab testing showing more than 90% accuracy. The target cost is under $25.

UNSW School of Systems and Computing Associate Professor Huadong Mo said as more electric vehicles (EVs) reach the end of their life, Australia has a real opportunity to build a local second-life battery industry, with retired batteries supporting grid and comunity energy storage.

“Up to 95% of a battery’s components can be recovered, some even to make new batteries. Yet only a small fraction of lithium-ion batteries in Australia are collected for recycling today,” Mo said.

The researchers have partnered with Malaysia-headquartered battery recycling and lifecycle management company DY New Energy on a $1.3 million project to test the new technology on more than 500 batteries in real-world conditions.

Before piloting it in recycling facilities and second-life battery storage systems, the DY and UNSW researchers will develop and test a machine learning-powered decision engine that recommends whether retired batteries should be reused or recycled.

A Battery Management System (iBMS) module will then integrate insights directly into battery systems for real-time monitoring and decision support.

UNSW School of Mathematics and Statistics, and Research Lead Dr Ziyang Lyu said recyclers rarely receive neatly sorted batches.

“One day it might be LFP cells, the next a mix of nickel-based chemistries from different manufacturers. We’ve designed our models to handle that variety, so the platform works with the batteries operators actually receive, not just ideal lab samples,” Lyu said.

Dr Lyu said the technology may also play a role in managing the growing number of batteries used in stationary energy storage systems.

“This technology could also support the future reuse and recycling of Australia’s rapidly expanding fleet of stationary energy storage systems, contributing to a more sustainable and circular battery economy.”

The project is also supported through the Trailblazer for Recycling and Clean Energy (TRaCE) Lab to Market Fund.

DY New Energy announced 13 November 2026 it will partner with the Australian Research Council’s (ARC’s) Fire Resilience Infrastructure, Assets and Safety Advancements (FRIASA) Hub to advance safe and scalable battery recycling.

item.title: Predicting power output from artistic BIPV pixel by pixel
item.dc:creator: Lior Kahana
item.description: Researchers have developed a model linking artwork colors to power output and potential hot-spot risks in colored BIPV arrays. Simulations of 50 masterpieces show how selectively darkening bright pixels can improve electrical performance.
item.content:encoded:
ASouth Korean research team has developed a novel model to predict power output and hot-spot risk in colored building-integrated PV (c-BIPV) systems featuring artistic images.

The researchers modeled PV arrays displaying 50 masterpieces, including Johannes Vermeer’s Girl with a Pearl Earring and Vincent van Gogh’s Café Terrace at Night.

“Unlike a uniformly colored module, an image-based array contains many differently colored cells. Because each color requires a different optical reflection profile, the photocurrent generated by each cell can vary across the array,” corresponding author Hyung-Jun Song told pv magazine.

“This spatial mismatch can reduce power output and, under certain bypass-diode configurations, expose cells to reverse bias and hot-spot risk.”

The novelty of the research, Song added, lies in directly linking the visual characteristics of a candidate image to the electrical performance and reliability of the entire PV array.

“For every pixel, we estimated the minimum-loss selective-reflection spectrum needed to reproduce its color and calculated the resulting photocurrent. We then used equivalent-circuit simulations to evaluate the series-connected array under different bypass-diode configurations,” he explained.

In its work, the group has converted each of the 50 artworks into a 36 × 36-pixel mosaic, with each of the 1,296 pixels representing an individual series-connected PV cell.

They assigned each pixel the average color of its corresponding image region. For each color, they calculated an ideal dual-band selective-reflection spectrum, selecting the reflection-band parameters that most closely reproduced the target color.

They then calculated the photocurrent generated from the sunlight transmitted through the colored layer, accounting for the underlying cell’s wavelength-dependent internal quantum efficiency.

Using a single-diode equivalent circuit calibrated to commercial TOPCon cells, they modeled each cell’s current-voltage characteristics at 300 K. They simulated the fully series-connected array in LTspice.

The simulations compared configurations without bypass diodes and with one diode protecting between one and 36 cells, assessing maximum power output and the number of cells operating under reverse bias at the maximum power point as an indicator of potential hot-spot risk.

“One of the most surprising findings was that the overall brightness or colorfulness of an image does not necessarily determine its photovoltaic performance. Instead, the spatial distribution of brightness plays a much more important role,” Song said about the results.

For example, the simulated array displaying Café Terrace at Night achieved 91.7% of the power output of an equivalent black reference array without bypass diodes, compared with 74.3% for Girl with a Pearl Earring.

“We found that even a small number of extremely bright pixels can limit the power output of an entire series-connected PV array,” the researcher added.

“We also identified an interesting trade-off associated with bypass diodes: installing more diodes can improve power output, but it may simultaneously increase reverse-bias conditions and the associated hot-spot risk.”

For Girl with a Pearl Earring, installing one bypass diode per cell increased normalised power from 74.3% to 84.4% of the black reference array’s output, a 13.6% relative improvement.

However, 24 of the 1,296 cells entered reverse bias at the maximum power point. Selectively darkening those 24 pixels instead raised normalised power to 84.8% without bypass diodes, while avoiding reverse-biased cells under the simulated conditions.

“Based on these findings, we developed a screening framework that classifies artistic images according to their expected power performance and hot-spot risk, using only two image-derived parameters: the brightest pixel and the overall brightness variation,” the academic added.

“The framework was further examined using additional images, demonstrating its potential to assess the electrical suitability of candidate artwork without requiring a full circuit-level simulation for every image.”

Concluding, Song said that his team is planning a few follow-up studies. These include incorporating measured reflectance spectra into a more realistic optical model, expanding the image database, and developing an AI-assisted tool to assess uploaded images and suggest modifications that improve power output and reduce hot-spot risks while preserving their appearance.

The article “Prediction Model for Power Output and Hot-spot Risk in Colored Photovoltaic Arrays with Artistic Image” has appeared in Energy. Researchers from South Korea’s Seoul National University of Science and Technology and Gachon University have participated in the study.

item.title: Australia’s battery manufacturing strength lays in component supply
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Prismatic battery cell cans from Australian aluminium and producing copper current collector foil, are both identified in a CSIRO report as front-runners for Australia's sovereign battery manufacturing capability.
item.content:encoded:
Prismatic battery cell cans from Australian aluminium using the impact extrusion process, and producing copper current collector foil using electrolytic deposition (ED), are both identified in a CSIRO report as front-runners for Australia’s sovereign battery manufacturing capability.

The future of Australian battery manufacturing: Cell cans and current collector foils report outlines a study focussed on the technical manufacturing processes and materials required for production of select components of lithium-ion battery cells: the battery cell cans and current collector foils used in each cell.

Comparing the requirements with known capabilities in Australia, the CSIRO researchers aimed to identify opportunities for a domestic battery supply chain

CSIRO Advanced Battery Manufacturing lead Dr Adam Best said Australia can bring more of the battery manufacturing value chain onshore.

“This would mean Australia could move beyond exporting raw and refined materials alone, towards creating higher-value products, supporting skilled manufacturing jobs and strengthening supply chains for technologies that will underpin the clean energy transition,” Best said.

Battery cell cans

On battery cell cans, the report’s primary recommendation is to first consider production of prismatic format battery cells made from Australian aluminium, using the impact extrusion route.

The researchers recommend that investment be made in an aluminium slug production facility equivalent to that commissioned by Jamestrong Packaging in 2025 for $6-$8 million (USD 4-5.4 million) but tailored to the requirements of prismatic cells.

Secondly, investment should be allocated to an automated, high volume, production cell specific to impact extrusion of prismatic type battery cell cans.

Production of foils

For Australian production of foils for battery cell current collectors, a first priority would be the production of copper foil in Australia using the ED method.

The report says it is the option more likely to offer a viable commercial case compared to rolled annealed (RA) copper foil or rolled aluminium foil.

Of the six recommendations for foil production, another includes the scoping and costing of an ED copper foil facility, in line with a scalable facility to enable a smaller up-front investment to reduce the barrier to entering the market, “but also offer scope for straightforward expansion of the production capacity by adding additional parallel production cells.”

CSIRO researcher Geoff de Looze said the study focused on realistic opportunities to move from minerals and materials into higher-value components.

“Australia has many of the building blocks needed for a battery manufacturing sector,” de Looze said.

item.title: Federal government cancels panel recycling pilot, considers ‘next steps’
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: The Australian government is considering 'next steps' for procuring a National Solar Panel Recycling Pilot administrator after cancelling the search on the same day an ongoing six month suspension of the procurement was also lifted.
item.content:encoded:
The Australian government is considering ‘next steps’ for procuring a National Solar Panel Recycling Pilot’ administrator, after cancelling its search the day an ongoing six month suspension was also lifted.

Undisclosed “changes to the industry” since the release of the government’s tender in April 2026, are cited as the catalyst for the decision on 10 November to cancel the procurement without the award of a contract.

Initially suspended in May 2026 due to a procurement complaint and consequent investigation, the original tender proposed that a contract for an NSPRP administrator would have begun by May 2026 and run until June 2027, with the possibility of extension.

The complaint centred on the settings and rules of the procurement process for the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW), but details are not public.

The $24.7 million (USD 16.9 million) pilot procurement sought to engage a supplier to arrange, manage, deliver and report to the government on an NSPRP.

It would be tasked with arranging the collection of up to 250,000 decommissioned panels from around 100 sites across Australia and ensure panels are safely aggregated, transported and recycled.

The government estimates 3 million panels reached end-of-life in 2025, and could grow to 50 million panels by 2035.
